S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral disturbances within three months of an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with distress out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation is heterogeneous and can include anxious, depressed, or mixed emotional features, as well as maladaptive behavioral responses such as withdrawal, conflict, or decline in role performance. By definition, the disturbance does not represent normal bereavement, does not meet criteria for another mental disorder, and symptoms do not persist for more than six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. It is often seen in the context of life transitions, interpersonal conflicts, health problems, or occupational stress, and is distinguished from more severe mood or anxiety disorders by its time-limited, stressor-linked course and relatively circumscribed impairment.

patient.personality: Eric is a competitive, structure‑driven professional who thrives on clear goals, order, and high performance, balancing intense work focus with organized social and athletic pursuits.
patient.stressor: Eric had carefully mapped out both his career trajectory toward a security manager role and a stable home life with his wife, with shared routines around church, soccer, and extended family gatherings, when his wife disclosed that she was unexpectedly pregnant at the same time she was considering relocating closer to her family for a job opportunity. The news collided with his tightly controlled financial planning and performance goals, as he worried about affording childcare, potentially starting over at a new casino, and losing the familiar support network and routines he believes keep him on track. Over the subsequent month, ongoing, unresolved conversations with his wife about whether to move, how to manage their schedules, and what compromises each would make began to feel like a constant pressure; at work he found himself increasingly preoccupied with fears of failing as a provider and partner, while at home he reacted to minor disagreements with an intensity that surprised even him, straining their relationship further. When his supervisor informally noted that he seemed unusually distracted on shift and his wife expressed concern that his stress over these changes was starting to dominate their interactions and decisions, Eric agreed to see a psychiatrist, recognizing that his way of responding to the situation was no longer constructive and was impairing both his performance and family life.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since my wife told me about the pregnancy and possible move, I feel like I’m reacting to the stress all wrong and it’s starting to mess up my work and home life.”

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.
S081.manifestation: Ever since all this came up, it’s like I flipped a switch into this tense, irritable mode where I’m snapping at my wife over little things, lying awake running numbers in my head instead of sleeping, zoning out on camera duty because I’m replaying our arguments about the move, and then hating myself afterward because I know I’m overreacting but I can’t seem to dial it back.
